title: Reasons of the heart
hookLine: Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know

lines: A NOTE SEWN INTO A COAT.
NOT THE GOD OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.
cards: After Blaise Pascal died, the story goes, a servant found a folded paper sewn into the lining of his coat. On it Pascal had written about one night when, as he tells it, he met God.

You met that night of fire in year three. Near the top, after the date, stands a single word: fire. It names the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, and adds: not of the philosophers and the scholars.
Pascal was a mathematician, a man of proofs. And a note with no proof in it was the one he kept in his coat.

teach.b: Pascal left behind a pile of notes for a book he never finished. They were gathered after his death as the Pensées, his thoughts. In one of them he writes: "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know."
The line often gets used to mean, feelings beat facts. Pascal meant something sharper. He trusted reason; he did mathematics.
But he noticed that some things we know without proving them: that we're awake and not dreaming, the first principles that all our proofs start from.

These, he said, we know by the heart, a kind of direct knowing underneath argument. And faith, for Pascal, lives there too. In another note he says it is the heart, not the reason, that perceives God.
That isn't giving up on thinking. It's honesty about where thinking starts. Scripture gives the heart that kind of weight.
Proverbs says, "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."
And when the shepherds have told what they saw at the manger, Luke says, "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart."
Pondering in the heart: not feeling instead of thinking, but thinking all the way down. Pascal's night of fire wasn't the end of an argument.

It was more like recognizing a voice in a crowded room before you can explain how you know it. And still he went on writing arguments, because for him the head and the heart were meant to work together.

how: Christians read Pascal's Pensées as a classic of faith and reason; across churches, Christians speak of knowing God with the heart as well as the mind, in prayer, worship, and quiet reflection.

games.q: what does “reasons of the heart” mean?
o: a prayer said with the heart instead of the lips
Pascal's idea that the heart knows what proof can't
the idea that feelings should always beat facts

games.q: the heart has reasons — tap the pairs.
p: keep thy heart with all diligence
Mary pondered them in her heart

s: "the heart has its reasons" means feelings beat facts

a man of proofs, who still wrote that the heart perceives God.

Luke 2:19: "Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart."

games.q: you're Pascal, a mathematician who trusts proofs. one night you meet God, and you can't prove it to anyone. what do you do with it?
o: throw it out, since it can't be proved.
write it down and keep it with you.
turn it into a mathematical proof.
games.why: the story goes his note was found sewn into his coat after he died: fire, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not of the philosophers.

practice: Bring to mind something you know but can't fully prove: that a certain person loves you, that a choice you made was right, that a place is home.
Don't argue for it; let it be known, the way Pascal said the heart knows, and notice whether it holds steady when you stop defending it. If you pray, you can bring that knowing to God and rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Reasons of the heart. Pascal's line: the heart knows some things, God among them, that reason can't reach by proof alone.
